meta.regime: The regime has rotated a third time in four sessions - from geopolitics to the Fed on Friday's payroll shock, and now back to geopolitics on a 5% crude surge. Trump demanded on Monday that Iran compensate victims' families and regional states, and Iran's Supreme National Security Council answered with the full list of its own conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz: lift the naval blockade, lift sanctions, withdraw US forces from the region, pay war reparations and release frozen Iranian assets. That is not a negotiating gap that closes this week, and the market has priced it - WTI and Brent both rose about 5%, taking WTI out of $78.82 into the low $80s and Brent from $84.18 to roughly $88, with Kpler reporting transit traffic through the strait subdued and weakening further into the weekend. The FX consequence is a clean terms-of-trade sort. Canada is the direct beneficiary and now has two legs at once, the +75,100 July jobs print and a crude bid, so CAD is upgraded from +1 to +2. Japan is the direct loser: USD/JPY is 158.77 against 157.80 yesterday, which means the yen weakened on a day the dollar had no good news, because a JPY 407bn trade deficit and terms of trade at 82.71 transmit an oil shock straight into the currency before the BoJ's 3.4% wage growth can help. JPY is downgraded from 0 to -1. The second event was the RBA: a hold at 4.35% that all 37 Reuters economists called correctly, but Bullock made it hawkish - the economy is operating ABOVE CAPACITY, growth needs to slow to tame inflation, and the statement retained 'including increasing the cash rate target further if required' with no softening. With Q2 weighted median CPI having RISEN to 3.7% and commodity prices up 15.4% y/y, AUD is upgraded to +2. The dollar is caught between two forces and stays at -1: July payrolls contracted 23,000 with the prior two months revised down and September hike odds at roughly 44%, but the dollar index firmed overnight and the ten-year is back near 4.6% because an oil shock is an inflation input. That tension resolves at 12:30Z tomorrow.

dailyRead: Oil is back in charge and it has reordered the board. Trump demanded on Monday that Iran compensate victims' families and Middle Eastern states as a condition for talks, and Tehran answered with its own list - reopening the Strait of Hormuz requires Washington to lift the naval blockade, lift sanctions, withdraw US forces from the region, pay war reparations and release frozen Iranian assets. Those two positions do not converge in a week, and crude repriced accordingly: WTI and Brent both rose about 5%, taking WTI out of $78.82 into the low $80s and Brent from $84.18 to roughly $88, with Kpler reporting transit traffic subdued and weakening further. This is a terms-of-trade shock, and it sorts the G10 cleanly. Canada is upgraded from +1 to +2 and is now the strongest currency on the board alongside the euro and the Aussie: it has the +75,100 July employment print, the largest gain in two years, unemployment at a two-year low of 6.4%, participation at 65.1%, AND a crude bid, with the only missing leg being rates - CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9% are both still below target so the BoC holds again on Sept 2. Japan is the mirror loser and the day's clearest downgrade: USD/JPY is 158.77 against 157.80, meaning the yen LOST ground on a session where the dollar had nothing good, because Japan is the G10's largest energy importer running a JPY 407bn trade deficit with terms of trade at 82.71, and an oil shock reaches the currency through the trade account long before the BoJ's 3.4% wage growth and 1.9% Tokyo core CPI can help it. JPY goes from 0 to -1, which makes CAD/JPY, EUR/JPY and AUD/JPY the cleanest yen shorts - but keep size disciplined, because 158.77 is walking back toward the 160 zone that drew the last joint MoF and US Treasury operation, and that reverses in minutes. The second event was the RBA. The hold at 4.35% was unanimous in the Reuters poll and delivered on schedule at 04:30Z, but Bullock made it hawkish: the economy is running ABOVE CAPACITY, growth needs to slow to bring inflation down, and the statement retained 'including increasing the cash rate target further if required' with no qualification - the cycle is explicitly not finished. That matters more than the rate, because the Q2 detail was already awkward for the doves: headline cooled to 3.8% but the weighted median ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5% and services inflation to 4.0%. Add commodity prices up 15.4% y/y and a crude rebound that removes the disinflationary Q3 assumption, and AUD is upgraded from +1 to +2. AUD/USD spiked below 0.7050 during the presser from Monday's 0.7075 highs and then recovered, which is the price action of a market that was already long the hawkish story. The euro holds +2 and the oil move helps rather than hurts it: Lagarde tied the hiking bias explicitly to the energy channel, euro-area energy inflation had already accelerated to 10.0% from 8.5% in July, and crude just went up another 5%, so the September 10 hike at roughly 70% priced is now better supported than it was yesterday, on top of July HICP 2.9% with core UP to 2.5%, services 3.3%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and composite PMI 52.0. Deposit rate stays 2.25%. Sterling holds +1 as the follower - the labour market report lands this morning and Q2 GDP on Thursday, and a net energy importer with the most inflation-sensitive committee in the G10, having gone 6-3 against a 7-2 consensus, keeps the hawkish tail alive rather than the dovish one. The dollar stays at -1 but the case is now genuinely two-sided. On the dovish side, July payrolls contracted 23,000 against +83k to +95k expected, the prior two months were revised down by a combined 146,000, unemployment fell to 4.1% only because participation collapsed to 61.4%, and average hourly earnings slowed to 3.2%, leaving September hike odds around 44%. On the hawkish side, the dollar index firmed overnight, the ten-year is back near 4.6%, and a 5% crude move is an inflation input into a CPI print that lands tomorrow at 12:30Z with consensus at 3.4% headline and 2.5% core. Do not add to dollar shorts into that number. New Zealand stays the anchor short at -2 and the oil move makes it worse in the most specific way possible - the Q2 CPI of 4.1% that forced July's hike was 27.5% petrol, so a renewed crude bid re-fires the exact inflation channel the RBNZ cannot answer with unemployment at a decade-high 5.6%, underutilisation at 13.8% and the labour cost index at 2.1%. EUR/NZD, AUD/NZD, GBP/NZD long and NZD/CAD short remain the highest-conviction structure on the board. The franc stays -1 on a zero policy rate with no path off it before 2027, July CPI 0.4% with core 0.3%, but the haven complex is bid on renewed escalation and SNB reserves rose to CHF 768.3bn in July, so franc shorts are for the crosses with a real rate story - CAD/CHF, EUR/CHF, AUD/CHF - and not for USD/CHF, which is a RANGE. In commodities, gold has rallied above $4,430 from $4,325 on haven demand, central-bank buying and collapsing US real-rate expectations and stays a HIGH conviction long; silver holds near $64 with the $65.21 level the bull trigger and $63.10 the bear one, so it stays LONG but at MEDIUM; USOIL is upgraded to a HIGH conviction long while the compensation impasse holds. GER40 stays RANGE - it is a record-high equity index that now faces both a hawkish ECB and a 5% energy cost shock. Everything reprices at 12:30Z tomorrow.

USD.note: Held 3.50-3.75% on Jul 29 for a fifth straight meeting with THREE dissents FOR a hike, and Chair Warsh declined to give guidance or submit a dot. Friday's payroll report undercut that case badly: July nonfarm payrolls CONTRACTED by 23,000 against +83,000 to +95,000 expected, the prior two months were revised down by a combined 146,000, June was cut to +20,000, and the fall in unemployment to 4.1% from 4.2% is a participation artefact with participation at a five-year low of 61.4%. Average hourly earnings slowed to 3.2% y/y, the weakest since May 2021. Rate futures now price roughly a 44% chance of a September hike against 57% before the release. What changed overnight is that the hawkish tail has been rebuilt from a different direction: a 5% crude surge is an inflation input, the dollar index firmed and the ten-year is back near 4.6%. The residual hawkish reads remain real - Lisa Cook said in Anchorage she is prepared to raise rates, initial claims are at a cycle-low four-week average of 198,750, announced layoffs are the lowest in two years and unit labour costs rose just 1.3%. June CPI 3.5%, core 2.6%, Q2 GDP 1.5%. July CPI on Aug 12 at 12:30Z, consensus 3.4% headline and 2.5% core, decides it.

EUR.when: Sept 10 (~70% priced, energy channel just reinforced)
EUR.note: Deposit facility 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike, headline refi 2.40% and marginal lending 2.65%, all confirmed unchanged on Jul 23. The ECB's July communication is the operative text and the oil move validates it: the Bank warned the full inflationary impact of the energy shock has yet to emerge, and Lagarde said the longer energy prices stay elevated the more likely they are to drive broader inflation through second-round effects. Euro-area energy inflation had already accelerated to 10.0% from 8.5% in July, and crude has now added another 5% on the Hormuz impasse - that channel is widening, not closing. The domestic leg stands on its own: July HICP 2.9% from 2.8% with core UP to 2.5%, services inflation 3.3%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, final composite PMI 52.0 with services 51.7 and manufacturing 51.9, wage growth 3.4%, unemployment 6.3%, ZEW economic sentiment 23.4 from 9.5. The counterargument is pipeline disinflation - producer prices decelerating to 4.6% y/y from 5.9%, food inflation at 1.2% and June retail sales falling 0.3% m/m - but an energy-led CPI overrides it in the ECB's own framing.

GBP.note: Held 3.75% on Jul 30 but 6-3, a third member joining the dissent against a 7-2 consensus. June CPI 2.6% with core 2.6% and services 3.6%. The labour market is firmer than the pause implies - employment +148k in May, wages 4.3% including bonuses and 3.4% excluding, unemployment 4.9% - and July PMIs were revised up again to services 52.1 and composite 52.2 from a sub-50 June. Q1 GDP was +0.6% q/q. The soft spots are the claimant count rising 6.7k, payrolled employees falling and manufacturing at 51.9. The crude surge matters here: a net energy importer facing a renewed oil bid with the most inflation-sensitive committee in the G10 keeps the hawkish tail alive rather than the dovish one, and TE's end-of-quarter forecast is 4.00%. The labour market report lands this morning and Q2 GDP on Aug 13 - those are the first real domestic inputs in two weeks.

JPY.note: Held 1.00% on Jul 31 8-1, Takata dissenting for 1.25%. The wage leg is intact - June labour cash earnings +3.4% y/y with base pay accelerating to 3.4% from 3.0%, real earnings positive for a sixth month, and nominal growth above 3% for five straight months, the longest run in 34 years. The Bank has warned for the first time that underlying inflation could exceed target and said discussions will focus on upside price risks. June CPI rose to 1.7% from 1.5% with core at 1.6%, and Tokyo July core CPI jumped to 1.9% from 1.6%. What is broken is the transmission to the currency. USD/JPY is 158.77 against 157.80 yesterday - the yen LOST ground on a session where the dollar had no good news, because a 5% crude surge hits a JPY 407bn trade deficit with terms of trade at 82.71 before any of the inflation case can help. This is why JPY is downgraded to -1 despite the best domestic wage story in three decades. Q2 GDP lands Aug 16 23:50Z. A second joint MoF and US Treasury operation, most likely if 160 trades, remains the fastest route to a yen repricing.

AUD.note: Held the cash rate at 4.35% on Aug 11 as all 37 Reuters economists and all four majors expected, but the tone did the work. Bullock said the domestic economy is operating ABOVE CAPACITY and that growth will need to slow to bring inflation down, and the statement retained the line 'including increasing the cash rate target further if required' with no qualification - the tightening cycle is explicitly not finished. That is the highest policy rate in the G10 after three hikes in 2026 (Feb 3.85%, Mar 4.10%, May 4.35%) on the energy shock. The Q2 detail supports the hawkish read: headline CPI cooled to 3.8% from 4.0% and trimmed mean held 3.6%, but the WEIGHTED MEDIAN ROSE to 3.7% from 3.5% and services inflation to 4.0%. Labour is solid with employment +76,343 in June, unemployment 4.4% and participation at 67.0%. July PMIs are strong at services 53.6, composite 53.2 and manufacturing 52.0, consumer confidence improved to 83.9, June trade swung to a AUD 1,929m surplus and commodity prices are +15.4% y/y. TE's model carries 4.60%. AUD/USD spiked below 0.7050 during the presser from Monday's 0.7075 highs and then recovered. The dovish input is July consumer inflation expectations collapsing to 4.7% from 5.5%.

NZD.note: OCR raised 25bp to 2.50% on Jul 8, the first hike in three years, and that cycle is finished. Q2 unemployment printed 5.6% against 5.4% expected, the highest since Q3 2015; underutilisation widened to 13.8%; the labour cost index slowed to 2.1% y/y; and employment rose 0.5% q/q only because participation climbed to 70.7% from 70.4%. The crude surge is uniquely bad here: the Q2 CPI of 4.1% that triggered July's move was 27.5% petrol, so a 5% oil move re-fires the exact imported-inflation channel New Zealand has no capacity to answer, with core at 3.2% and gasoline already at USD 1.70 a litre. The offset is domestic sentiment, which keeps improving: July ANZ business confidence 56.1 from 36.6, ANZ Roy Morgan consumer confidence 99.3 from 91.3, manufacturing PMI 59.7 and composite 53.6. Two-year inflation expectations 2.53%; the RBNZ survey lands Aug 13.

CAD.note: Held 2.25% on Jul 15 for a sixth straight meeting, and neither the July labour report nor the oil move changes that, because the inflation side is still undershooting - June CPI 2.8% with CPI-trim at 1.8% and CPI-median at 1.9%, both BELOW target, and core at 2.1%. Everything else has changed. July employment rose 75,100, the largest gain in two years, with full-time +38,600, part-time +36,600, unemployment falling to a two-year low of 6.4% from 6.5% and participation rising to 65.1%; core-aged women's unemployment fell 0.3pp to 5.2% and youth unemployment dropped to 12.6% from an April peak of 14.3%. Average hourly wages rose a soft 2.8% y/y to $37.17, which is why this stays a growth upgrade rather than a rate one. Now add a 5% crude surge on top of three prior up sessions, taking WTI out of $78.82 into the low $80s with Brent near $88, and the loonie has a labour leg and a terms-of-trade leg simultaneously. That is what takes CAD to +2. Q1 GDP was flat at 0.0% q/q with monthly GDP +0.2% in June.

CHF.note: At ZERO since mid-2025, held Dec, Mar and Jun; panellists see no change until 2027. July CPI came in at 0.4% y/y against 0.5% expected, down from 0.5%, with core unchanged at 0.3% - under the SNB's own 0.7% Q3 conditional forecast. July unemployment rose to 3.0% from 2.9% with unemployed persons at 139,276, adding a growth argument to the inflation undershoot, and producer and import prices are deflating at -2.1% y/y. The June statement pledged to lean against rapid APPRECIATION only, so the SNB is content to let the franc slide. Two things argue caution on pressing franc shorts, and the escalation makes them heavier today: FX reserves rose to CHF 768.3bn in July from 758.9bn, and the haven complex is bid with gold above $4,430 on the Hormuz impasse. The domestic activity data is also turning up hard - services PMI at 63.9 from 59.8, business confidence 104 and ZEW economic sentiment flipping to +10 from -25. Trade the franc through crosses with a real rate or terms-of-trade story, not through USD/CHF.

catalysts.event: MoF / US Treasury yen intervention watch
catalysts.note: USD/JPY at 158.77 and rising on the oil move. The last joint operation spiked it to 155.20. Above 160 the risk is not technical - it is a second official operation that reverses every yen cross in minutes.

Both expected to hold, at 2.25% and 2.50%. Canada's core measures are still below target and New Zealand's cycle is finished - neither is a rates event, but the statements set the tone for the NZD/CAD structure.

geopolitics: The oil channel reopened today and it is the dominant FX input. Trump demanded on Monday that Iran compensate victims' families and Middle Eastern countries as a precondition for talks, after Tehran said it would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz without being compensated for war damage. Iran's Supreme National Security Council then set out the full price: lift the naval blockade, lift sanctions, withdraw US military forces from the region, pay war reparations and release frozen Iranian assets. Those positions do not converge quickly, and crude repriced about 5% on the recognition - WTI out of $78.82 into the low $80s, Brent from $84.18 to roughly $88. The negotiating track that had been driving optimism is narrower than it looked: Iran and Oman have agreed the coordinates of a safe corridor and Araghchi has called the draft very close, but the IRGC has been explicit that reopening the strait has its own mechanism, separate from the Oman negotiation, and requires Washington to accept Iran's conditions in full. The crisis has been running since Feb 28 with at least twelve seafarers killed or missing, and Kpler reports transit traffic subdued over the past week and weakening further into the weekend. Iran has also hardened its command structure - Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei announced six senior military appointments including Ali Abdollahi as armed forces chief of staff, and a hardline former Revolutionary Guard commander now holds the top security post - while the UAE reported an Iranian missile strike on an ADNOC-linked vessel. The FX transmission is a clean terms-of-trade sort. Canada is the direct winner and is upgraded to +2, with the crude bid landing on top of a +75,100 employment print. Japan is the direct loser and is downgraded to -1: USD/JPY moved from 157.80 to 158.77 on a session where the dollar had nothing good, because a JPY 407bn trade deficit and terms of trade at 82.71 transmit an energy shock straight into the currency. New Zealand is the second loser through a different door, since 27.5% of the Q2 CPI that forced July's hike was petrol and there is no policy capacity left to answer it. The euro is a beneficiary rather than a victim because the ECB has explicitly tied its hiking bias to the energy channel, and the franc and gold both hold a haven bid - gold above $4,430 - which is why franc shorts belong in the crosses and not against the dollar. The single headline that reverses all of it is a signed transit mechanism, and it would remove the premium faster than the market added it.
